cards.title: Generator Expression
cards.teaser: A memory-efficient alternative to a list comprehension — uses parentheses instead of brackets and returns an iterator rather than building the whole list in memory.

runs.text: A list comprehension evaluates every element immediately and stores the result in memory. A
generator expression
does neither: it creates a lazy iterator that produces one value at a time, on demand. The syntax is identical except for the delimiters — square brackets become parentheses.

Why this matters at scale: loading a 10 GB log file with a list comprehension allocates 10 GB of RAM. A generator expression allocates a few hundred bytes for the iterator object and reads one line per iteration. The processing time is roughly the same; the memory profile is not.

items.text: List comprehension:
`[x * 2 for x in range(1_000_000)]` — allocates one million integers.
Generator expression:
`(x * 2 for x in range(1_000_000))` — allocates one integer at a time.

runs.text: Generator expressions can be chained: `sum(x * 2 for x in range(1_000_000))` passes the expression directly to `sum()` without parentheses because it's already inside a function call — Python lets you drop the extra pair.
Default to generator expressions when you only need to iterate once. Reach for a list when you need random access, len(), or need to iterate multiple times.
A list comprehension is a photocopier making all the copies at once. A generator expression is a person handing you one page at a time as you read it. Same pages, very different memory bill.

cards.title: yield Keyword
cards.teaser: The keyword that turns a plain function into a generator function — execution pauses at each `yield`, resumes on the next call to `next()`, and the local state is preserved in between.

runs.text: When Python sees the
yield
keyword inside a function body, it classifies that function as a generator function. Calling it does not execute the body — it returns a generator object. The body starts running only when you call
next()
on that object, and it pauses again the moment it hits the next `yield`, handing back the yielded value.
All local variables and the execution position are frozen between yields. This makes generator functions the natural fit for:

items.text: Infinite sequences
— `while True: yield value` runs forever without consuming memory.
Lazy file reading
— yield one line at a time instead of `readlines()` into a list.
State machines
— local state persists between yields without a class.

runs.text: A generator is exhausted when the function body returns (or falls off the end). Calling `next()` after that raises `StopIteration`, which is what a `for` loop uses internally to know when to stop.
Generator functions are not coroutines — they produce values. Async coroutines consume values from an event loop. The `yield` keyword predates `async/await` and serves a different purpose.

Imagine a chef who preps one dish, rings the bell, and waits. Not sleeping, not gone — just frozen mid-motion, ready to resume the moment the server picks up the plate. That is yield: a deliberate pause that preserves all the work in progress.

cards.title: yield from
cards.teaser: Delegates iteration to a sub-generator — cleaner than a for loop, and the only way to transparently forward `send()` and `throw()` calls into the inner generator.

runs.text: Before
yield from

(PEP 380), composing generators required a loop: `for item in sub: yield item`. That works for simple cases but silently breaks bidirectional communication — any `send()` or `throw()` values directed at the outer generator are never forwarded to the inner one.
`yield from iterable` does everything the loop does, and more:

items.text: Yields every item from the sub-iterable transparently.
Forwards `send()` values down into the sub-generator.
Forwards `throw()` and `close()` calls as well.
Captures the sub-generator's return value
as the result of the `yield from` expression itself.

runs.text: The practical everyday use: flattening nested iterables cleanly. `yield from chain` or `yield from sublist` reads like English and signals delegation rather than manual iteration.
When refactoring a large generator into smaller helpers, use `yield from helper()` to compose them. The caller sees a single seamless stream.
It is a call-forwarding service. When someone calls the outer generator, `yield from` patches the call through to the inner one without either side noticing the middleman.

cards.title: Iterator Protocol
cards.teaser: The two-method contract (`__iter__` and `__next__`) that any object must satisfy to work inside a `for` loop, `zip()`, `map()`, or any other iteration context.

runs.text: Python's `for` loop is syntactic sugar over two steps: call
__iter__()
to get an iterator, then repeatedly call
__next__()
until `StopIteration` is raised. Any object that implements both methods satisfies the iterator protocol.

items.text: __iter__(self)
— returns the iterator object itself. For an iterator, `return self`. For a container (list, set), returns a fresh iterator over its contents.
__next__(self)
— returns the next value, or raises `StopIteration` when exhausted.

runs.text: The key distinction: iterables (lists, strings, dicts) have `__iter__` and produce a new iterator each time. Iterators are stateful — they can only be traversed once. Passing a generator to two `for` loops results in an empty second loop, not two full iterations.

If your function receives an argument and iterates over it twice (once to validate, once to process), accept an iterable but call `list()` on it first — or explicitly document that the caller must not pass a one-shot iterator.

A playlist is iterable — you can start it over any time. A cassette tape is an iterator — it remembers where the read head is, you can only go forward, and rewinding is not guaranteed. Python's `for` loop works with both; the difference only bites you when you try to play the tape twice.

cards.title: itertools Module
cards.teaser: The standard-library toolkit for combining, slicing, and transforming iterators without materializing intermediate lists — `chain`, `islice`, `groupby`, `takewhile`, `product`, and more.

runs.text: The
itertools

module is the functional programming companion to Python's iterator protocol. Every function in it returns an iterator — no intermediate lists are allocated, which means the combinatorics stay O(1) in memory even when they produce millions of combinations.
Key tools by category:

items.text: Combining:
`chain(a, b)` concatenates iterables; `zip_longest(a, b)` handles uneven lengths.
Slicing:
`islice(it, stop)` takes up to N items without indexing; `dropwhile` / `takewhile` slice by predicate.
Grouping:
`groupby(it, key)` collapses consecutive equal-key items — requires sorted input if you want all groups.
Combinatorics:
`product`, `permutations`, `combinations` — generate Cartesian products and selections lazily.
Infinite:
`count(start)`, `cycle(it)`, `repeat(val, n)` — all require external termination (islice, takewhile).

runs.text: Before writing a custom loop to combine iterators, search itertools first. If itertools doesn't have it, check `more-itertools` (third-party) — the pattern you need likely already exists and is tested.
itertools is a set of Lego connectors for iterators. You don't build data; you build plumbing. The data flows through without ever pooling in a lake.

cards.title: Generator send() Method
cards.teaser: Pushes a value into a paused generator at the `yield` point — turning a one-way producer into a two-way channel, and the foundation for coroutine-style programming before `async/await`.

runs.text: A `yield` expression has two roles. It
emits
a value out of the generator (the right-hand side of `yield value`) and it
receives
a value from the caller (the result the `yield` expression evaluates to). The `send()` method is the mechanism for that second direction.
Usage pattern:

items.text: Advance to the first yield with `next(gen)` or `gen.send(None)`
— you must prime the generator before sending a real value.
Call `gen.send(value)` to resume the generator with `value` as the result of the yield expression.
The generator runs until the next `yield`, which becomes the return value of `send()`.

runs.text: This bidirectional channel was used to implement cooperative multitasking before `asyncio` — Twisted and Tornado both exploited it. In modern Python, `async/await` is cleaner for that use case, but `send()` remains valuable for stateful stream processors: running average calculators, pipelines that accept configuration mid-stream, or teaching how event loops work.
The must-prime requirement is a common bug. Wrap generator-coroutines in a decorator that auto-advances to the first yield, or document the priming requirement explicitly.

Normally a generator is like a vending machine: you press a button (next()) and get a snack. send() makes it a two-way kiosk — you insert a coin (the value) and it uses it to decide what snack to dispense next.

cards.title: Comprehension Complexity Threshold
cards.teaser: Comprehensions are readable when they map a single expression — once they contain nested loops, multiple conditions, or side effects, a plain `for` loop is almost always clearer.

runs.text: Comprehensions offer a compact, declarative syntax that communicates intent in one line. But compactness and clarity are not the same thing. When a comprehension grows beyond two clauses, it starts requiring more mental parse cycles than the equivalent loop — and it stops being self-documenting.
The signals that a comprehension has crossed the threshold:

items.text: Two or more nested `for` clauses
— `[x for row in matrix for x in row if x > 0]` is readable; add another level and it collapses.
Multiple `if` filters
— stacking conditions obscures which applies where.
Non-trivial expression
— if the value expression needs a function call and two operations, extract a helper.
Side effects
— comprehensions that call `print()` or mutate state are a code smell; they imply you want a loop.

runs.text: Slatkin's rule of thumb: if the comprehension does not fit on one screen line without wrapping, turn it into a named loop with a comment. The overhead is three or four extra lines. The gain is that the next reader (including future you) understands it without a diagram.
One filter clause and one transformation is the sweet spot. Two for clauses are acceptable for matrix flattening. Beyond that, reach for a loop.
A comprehension is a one-liner on a sticky note. The moment it wraps onto a second sticky note, stop and write it on proper paper with real sentences. The goal was always clarity, not brevity.

cards.title: Memory Efficiency of Generators vs Lists
cards.teaser: A list holds every element in RAM simultaneously; a generator holds only enough state to produce the next one — a distinction that ranges from irrelevant to critical depending on data size.

runs.text: For a list of ten integers, the difference between a generator and a list is unmeasurable. For a 50 GB CSV, the difference is whether the program runs at all. Understanding
when
the difference matters is the skill.

items.text: Fixed, small data:
use a list. Random access, len(), slicing, and multiple iterations are all free.
Large or unbounded streams:
use a generator. Memory stays proportional to pipeline state, not input size.
Network or disk I/O:
generators match production rate to consumption rate, preventing buffer bloat.
One-pass transformations:
`sum()`, `max()`, `min()`, `any()`, `all()` all accept iterators — no list needed.

runs.text: The practical check: if you call `list()` on a generator immediately after creating it, you have not gained anything. The generator pays off only when you consume it incrementally — through a loop, a reducer function, or another generator stage.

Profile before assuming generators are faster. They avoid memory allocation but add per-item function call overhead. For tiny datasets, the list is often faster in CPU terms. The memory win is what matters at scale.

A list is a warehouse full of boxes. A generator is a conveyor belt that produces one box at a time as needed. The conveyor belt does not run out of floor space no matter how many boxes it eventually produces.

cards.title: next() with Default
cards.teaser: The built-in `next(iterator, default)` form retrieves the next item or returns a fallback instead of raising `StopIteration` — the safe way to peek at or consume the first item of an iterator.

runs.text: The two-argument form of
next()

— `next(iterator, default)` — is one of Python's under-used features. Without it, safely consuming the first item of a potentially-empty iterator requires a try/except block. With it, the pattern collapses to one expression.
Common patterns:

items.text: First match from a filter:
`next((u for u in users if u.is_admin), None)` — returns the first admin or None.
Peeking without consuming:
`itertools.chain([first], rest)` lets you look ahead and put the item back.
Sentinels:
`_MISSING = object()` then `val = next(it, _MISSING)` lets you distinguish 'no item' from 'item is None'.

runs.text: The single-argument form `next(it)` raises `StopIteration` on an empty iterator — legitimate in generator internals but a confusing crash in application code. Prefer the two-argument form whenever you cannot guarantee the iterator is non-empty.

In Python 3.7+, an unhandled `StopIteration` propagating out of a generator body is converted to a `RuntimeError`. This prevents a subtle bug where a called function's exhaustion silently terminates the outer generator.

`next(it, default)` is a polite request: "give me the next item if you have one; if not, here is what I will accept instead." The single-argument form is the same request with no backup plan — fine if you are certain, catastrophic if you are not.

cards.title: Generator Pipeline
cards.teaser: A chain of generator functions where each stage consumes an iterator and yields a transformed one — the Unix-pipe model for Python data processing, with memory capped at pipeline depth rather than dataset size.

runs.text: A
generator pipeline

is a sequence of generator functions where each stage wraps the previous one's output. The key property: no stage runs ahead of the consumer. When the final stage requests one item, the request propagates back through the chain, pulling exactly one item through each stage.
A canonical three-stage pipeline:

items.text: Source:
`lines = read_log(path)` — yields one line at a time from a file.
Transform:
`parsed = parse_records(lines)` — parses each line into a dict.
Filter:
`errors = filter_errors(parsed)` — yields only records with level == ERROR.

runs.text: Consuming with `for record in errors` drives all three stages. Memory usage is bounded by the size of one record, not one file. Adding a fourth stage is a one-line change that does not require restructuring the others.
Pipelines also compose with `itertools.chain` and `itertools.islice` for concatenation and early termination without modifying the individual stage functions.
Name each pipeline stage as a verb: `read_`, `parse_`, `filter_`, `transform_`. The call chain then reads like a sentence describing the data flow.

It is an assembly line where each station does exactly one job and passes one part to the next station on request. The factory floor never fills up with half-processed parts because no station stockpiles — it just waits for the next pull.

cards.title: Set Comprehension
cards.teaser: A concise way to build a set from an iterable using `{expr for item in iterable}` — automatically deduplicates and signals that uniqueness is the intent, not just an implementation detail.

runs.text: A
set comprehension

uses curly braces with a single expression — the same syntax as a dict comprehension minus the colon. The result is an unordered collection of unique values. It is semantically equivalent to `set(x for x in iterable)` but reads more directly.

items.text: Set comprehension:
`{ext for f in files for ext in [f.split('.')[-1]]}` — unique extensions.
Dict comprehension:
`{k: v for k, v in pairs}` — note the key: value form.
Empty set:
use `set()`, not `{}` — the empty brace literal creates an empty dict.

runs.text: The communicative value of a set comprehension: it makes the deduplication visible in the type itself. A reader seeing `{...}` knows immediately that duplicates are not preserved, without having to inspect whether `list()` or `set()` wraps the result.

Performance note: membership testing in a set is O(1) on average. If you build a comprehension and then repeatedly check `item in result`, a set comprehension is materially faster than a list comprehension for large inputs.
Set comprehensions require hashable elements. Attempting `{[1,2] for ...}` raises `TypeError`. Use frozenset if you need to contain mutable-equivalent items.

A set comprehension is a list comprehension that runs through a stamp collector: every duplicate gets tossed before it goes in the album. The curly braces tell the reader 'duplicates don't survive this' without needing a comment.

cards.title: Nested Comprehensions
cards.teaser: Multiple `for` clauses inside a single comprehension flatten or cross-join sequences — powerful when used for one level of nesting, but a readability trap the moment a second level is added.

runs.text: Python allows multiple `for` and `if` clauses in a single comprehension. They execute left-to-right, outermost first — the same order as nested `for` loops. A
nested comprehension
is not a comprehension that contains another comprehension; it is a comprehension with multiple `for` clauses.
The one-level case is fine:

items.text: Matrix flattening:
`[cell for row in matrix for cell in row]` — clear, conventional, widely understood.
Cartesian product:
`[(x, y) for x in xs for y in ys]` — equivalent to `itertools.product(xs, ys)`, readable at small scale.

runs.text: The two-level case usually is not fine. Three `for` clauses require the reader to mentally simulate a triple-nested loop while parsing a single expression. The resulting cognitive load is not worth the line savings. The equivalent explicit loops are not verbose — they are clear.
There is also a visual confusion trap: `[[x for x in row] for row in matrix]` is a comprehension that
contains

another comprehension as its value expression. This produces a list of lists. It looks similar to a multi-clause comprehension but is structurally different. Keeping them visually distinct prevents bugs.
Rule of thumb from Effective Python: two for clauses maximum. If you need a third, write a function with a name that explains what the nesting does, then call it from a single-clause comprehension.

One nesting level is a table — you scan left to right, then down. Two nesting levels are a Rubik's cube — you have to track three axes at once while reading a single sentence. The cube is not wrong; it just does not belong in a sentence.
